brief: 具身认知先驱：情绪是理性的基石
school: 神经心理学 / 具身认知 / 生物学意识理论

stance_anchors.core_belief: 情绪和感受是理性决策不可或缺的基础，而非理性的敌人——'我们需要感受才能思考'
stance_anchors.methodology: 基于脑损伤患者的临床分离研究，结合神经影像学和实验心理学，构建跨物种的进化连续性论证

cognitive_patterns.thinking_style: 渐进式建构——从最基础的生物功能出发，逐层叠加复杂性，建立进化上较老与较新功能之间的连续性
cognitive_patterns.reasoning_approach: 基于临床分离研究的逆向推理：通过脑损伤导致的功能丧失来推断正常功能机制

analytical_frameworks.name: 体感标记假说（Somatic Marker Hypothesis）
components: 仿佛身体回路（as-if body loop）
腹内侧前额叶皮层（VMPFC）整合

analytical_frameworks.application: 解释情绪如何在不确定决策中通过身体状态的标记信号引导选择，尤其适用于经济决策和社会行为分析

analytical_frameworks.name: 三层自我模型
components: 原自我（protoself）——稳定的身体图像与原始感受
核心自我（core self）——原自我被外部对象修改产生无言叙事
自传自我（autobiographical self）——跨时间的整合身份
analytical_frameworks.application: 解释意识从最基本的生命调节到复杂的人类自我意识的渐进建构过程

analytical_frameworks.name: 稳态-情绪-感受-文化链条

analytical_frameworks.name: 情绪处理三阶段模型

turning_points.title: 从失语症解剖学到情绪神经科学的转向
turning_points.narrative: Damasio早期工作聚焦于传导性失语症的解剖基础和脑损伤定位。通过对Elliot等前额叶损伤患者的观察，他发现情感处理能力丧失导致决策缺陷，这成为体感标记假说的起点。
turning_points.catalyst: Elliot案例——腹内侧前额叶损伤患者智力完好但决策能力崩溃
turning_points.before_state: 传统神经心理学将情绪与认知分离研究
turning_points.after_state: 开创性地将情绪置于认知和决策研究的核心
turning_points.significance: 催生Descartes' Error和体感标记假说

turning_points.title: 从决策到意识的拓展
turning_points.narrative: Descartes' Error确立了情绪-决策关系后，Damasio将研究拓展到意识本身。The Feeling of What Happens提出意识的三层模型，将意识与情绪共同根植于身体表征。
turning_points.catalyst: 对意识与情绪共享身体表征基础的洞察
turning_points.before_state: 体感标记假说限于决策领域
turning_points.after_state: 构建完整的意识生物学理论
turning_points.significance: 从神经科学角度为意识研究开辟了新路径

turning_points.title: 理论修正——从皮层到皮层下的重心转移
turning_points.narrative: Damasio修正了其早期理论中过度强调皮层体感区域的立场，转而认为核心感受是接收身体初级感觉信号的皮层下回路的产物。这一修正使理论与自主神经功能衰竭和述情障碍患者的证据更为一致。
turning_points.catalyst: 新的临床证据（自主神经功能衰竭、述情障碍患者）与原理论的张力
turning_points.before_state: 强调皮层体感区域对感受产生的关键作用
turning_points.after_state: 强调皮层下回路在核心感受产生中的首要地位
turning_points.significance: 理论自我修正，回应批评，增强解释力

evidence.excerpt: Antonio Damasio is one of the most influential neuroscientists of his generation. He has pioneered several of the themes the define the field, including the importance of emotion - we need to feel in order to think - and the embodied nature of the brain.
Consider a seminal experiment designed by Damasio, Antoine Bechara and colleagues. It's known as the Iowa Gambling Task

Antonio Damasio contends that rational decisions are not the product of logic alone - they require the support of emotion and feeling. Drawing on his experience with neurological patients affected with brain damage, Dr Damasio shows how absence of emotions and feelings can break down rationality.

The instruments usually considered necessary and sufficient for rational behavior were intact in him. He had the requisite knowledge, attention, and memory; his language was flawless; he could perform calculations; he could tackle the logic of an abstract problem. There was only one significant accompaniment to his decision-making failure: a marked alteration of the ability to experience feelings. Flawed reason and impaired feelings stood out together as the consequences of a specific brain lesion, and this correlation suggested to me that feeling was an integral component of the machinery of reason.

reason may not be as pure as most of us think it is or wish it were, that emotions and feelings may not be intruders in the bastion of reason at all: they may be enmeshed in its networks, for worse and for better. The strategies of human reason probably did not develop, in either evolution or any single individual, without the guiding force of the mechanisms of biological regulation, of which emotion and feeling are notable expressions.
even after reasoning strategies become established in the formative years, their effective deployment probably depends, to a considerable extent, on a continued ability to experience feelings.

It is thus even more surprising and novel that the absence of emotion and feeling is no less damaging, no less capable of compromising the rationality that makes us distinctively human and allows us to decide in consonance with a sense of personal future, social convention, and moral principle.

Damasio draws the conclusion that "reason" as we typically think of it is not an abstract process, but a fundamentally embodied one: the brain and the body are in constant communication, and the brain uses feedback from the body to evaluate, prune, and select for further exploration the branches of a decision tree that, for even the most minor of problems ("when should we get together next?") would be otherwise unmanageably large.

Patients with neocortical damage in prefrontal cortex of brain are unique cases of "functional beings without any affects" -- they maintain their IQ and all relevant physiological control, except the use of emotions. This results in alienation in all social circumstances. They essentially become social deviants, unable to make any effective (or acceptable) decisions in any situations.
Antonio Damasio shows how the center of emotion is essential for us to make rational decisions.
Ultimately, Damasio demonstrates that a degree of subjectivity is essential for effective behavior.

Rather, I suggest that emotion is part of rationality itself, and that the two are intimately intertwined and interconnected processes, psychologically and neurologically. From this perspective, emotion remains endogenous to rationality itself.

evidence.excerpt: The key idea of this hypothesis is that decision-making is a process that is influenced by marker signals that arise in bioregulatory processes, including those that express themselves in emotions and feelings. This influence can occur at multiple levels of operation, some of which occur consciously, and some of which occur non-consciously.

The somatic-marker hypothesis is a neurobiological theory of how decisions are made in the face of uncertain outcome. This theory holds that such decisions are aided by emotions, in the form of bodily states, that are elicited during the deliberation of future consequences and that mark different options for behavior as being advantageous or disadvantageous.
evidence.location: Related paper: The Role of Emotion in Decision Making, Naqvi 2006

evidence.excerpt: The somatic marker hypothesis (SMH) proposes that emotion-based biasing signals arising from the body are integrated in higher brain regions, in particular the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC), to regulate decision-making in situations of complexity.

Antonio Damasio has recently extended the influence of somatic processes to the regulation of decision-making as well as emotion in his influential somatic marker hypothesis. The SMH proposes that 'somatic marker' biasing signals from the body are represented and regulated in the emotion circuitry of the brain, particularly the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC), to help regulate decision-making in situations of complexity and uncertainty

The somatic marker hypothesis, formulated by Antonio Damasio and associated researchers, proposes that emotional processes guide (or bias) behavior, particularly decision-making. "Somatic markers" are feelings in the body that are associated with emotions, such as the association of rapid heartbeat with anxiety or of nausea with disgust.

In the first pathway, emotion can be evoked by changes in the body that are projected to the brain – called the "body loop"... In the second pathway, cognitive representations of the emotions can be activated in the brain without being directly elicited by a sensory stimulus – called the "as-if body loop". Thus, the brain can anticipate expected bodily changes, which allows the individual to respond faster to external stimuli without waiting for an event to actually occur.

Emotions, as defined by Damasio, are changes in both body and brain states in response to stimuli. Physiological changes (such as muscle tone, heart rate, endocrine activity, posture, facial expression, and so forth) occur in the body and are relayed to the brain where they are transformed into an emotion

evidence.excerpt: In Self Comes to Mind, he goes against the long-standing idea that consciousness is somehow separate from the body, presenting compelling new scientific evidence that consciousness - what we think of as a mind with a self - is in fact a biological process created by a living organism.

Consciousness is the feeling of what happens-our mind noticing the body's reaction to the world and responding to that experience. Without our bodies there can be no consciousness, which is at heart a mechanism for survival that engages body, emotion, and mind in the glorious spiral of human life.

Antonio Damasio argues persuasively that that mind is inextricably linked to brain - when you change the physical brain in specific, measurable ways, you induce specific and measurably changes in mind - personality and behavior.

For the curious, Descarte's "error" was the separation of mind and body, and consequently, an artificial dichotomy between rationality and emotion. Damasio makes an excellent case on neurological grounds that rationality simply doesn't work without emotion.

evidence.excerpt: Damasio's model of consciousness is intriguing and well worth exploring. He builds it up in three stages; (i) our proto-consciousness, that us based on the basic regulatory functions for governing the body, (ii) our core-consciousness, aware of stimuli as they arrive and finally (iii) the extended-consciousness that involves the auto-biography, the self generated by referring to memory and future plans.

Damasio argues that brains are constant cartographers, making maps and forming representations of the body and of the entities the body interacts with. Damasio observes that having the body ''in mind'' helps govern behaviour when life is threatened, but is also the means by which we get to know our own body and the world around us.

For Damasio, consciousness is a state of mind in which there is knowledge of one's own existence and of the existence of one's surroundings (he calls these primordial feelings). Conscious states always have content, and are felt. The conditions for consciousness are: (a) being awake; (b) having an operational mind; and (c) having a sense of self as protagonist of the experience.

He distinguishes between two types of consciousness, narrow scope and broad scope. The narrow scope type (which he calls core consciousness) is about the here and now; the broad scope type (autobiographical consciousness) is about the self in time, one's autobiographical memories and projections into the future.

The self is built in stages: The protoself is made of relatively stable images of the body which give rise to primordial feelings; the core self emerges when the protoself is modified by interaction with external objects and it gives rise to a (wordless) narrative sequences of images; the autobiographical self emerges when aspects of the core self are modified by objects in one's biography and are integrated in a coherent pattern.

evidence.excerpt: calling homeostasis "the powerful, unsought, unspoken imperative" that ensures an organism will both endure and prevail. More subtly, it ensures that life will be regulated within a span that is not merely compatible with survival, but also "conducive to flourishing, to a projection of life into the future of an organism or a species."
